extracted.intended_audience: photographers, anthropologists, and scientists interested in photographic composite-portrait methods and phenotypic/statistical typology
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and methodological guidance for producing optical and photographic composite portraits (superimposing multiple photographs to obtain an averaged "type") and guidance on instruments, exposures, registration, weighting, and suitable uses (racial types, criminal types, family heredity, historical likenesses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Component similarity in attitude and size
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect photographs of the persons with whom you propose to deal. They must be similar in attitude and size, but no exactness is necessary in either of these respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components should be roughly same size and attitude so that when superimposed the eyes and other features approximately coincide. Slight differences can be compensated later by lenses, foreshortening, or placing larger photographs farther from the eye; exact identity is not required but similarity improves composite quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and placement of register-marks (pinholes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make two pinholes in each photograph to enable hanging them one in front of the other upon the same pair of pins so that the eyes of all the portraits shall be as nearly as possible superimposed; these pinholes correspond to 'register-marks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a slip of brass or card with an aperture and cross-threads to align pupils, then prick through holes. Register marks permit mechanically consistent alignment; they may be made in the case rather than on the photographs themselves. Needles in a hinged arm may be used to register any desired feature (nose, ear, hand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential photographic exposure of components (equal-time composite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Throw faint images of the several portraits, in succession, upon the same sensitized photographic plate; e.g., if an exact copy requires eighty seconds and there are eight portraits, expose each for ten seconds in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total exposure equals sum of exposures of components. It is better to allow equal time to all components; unequal exposure or ordering (giving later components longer exposure) can bias the composite. Exposure times may be varied to 'weight' components deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting components by exposure or illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: It is perfectly easy to apportion different 'weights' to the different components: if one statue or portrait is judged more worthy of reliance it may receive double consideration by doubling its exposure time or illumination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportionate periods of exposure to give relative weights. Example provided: computing seconds per component when total desired exposure is known (see worked example with brothers/cousins). Weighting is the practical way to reflect differing reliability or relationship degrees in genealogical composites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mechanical/photographic precision over subjective artistic averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of the photographic composite is its mechanical precision, being subject to no errors beyond those incidental to all photographic productions. A composite portrait represents the picture that would rise before the mind's eye of a man who had the gift of pictorial imagination in an exalted degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographic composites avoid individual artist bias and produce repeatable, statistically grounded 'types'. Beware that artistic reproductions (e.g., wood-engraver renditions) may reintroduce bias and make the composite resemble a single component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: darkest outlines/shadows correspond to most common features; blur measures deviation
rubrics_metrics.description: Those of its outlines are sharpest and darkest that are common to the largest number of the components; the band will be darkest in its middle whenever the component portraits have the same general type of features, and its breadth or amount of blur will measure the tendency of the components to deviate from the common type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree of blur and darkness as diagnostic indicators: sharp/dark features = prevalent/common traits; broad/blurred outlines = variability among components. The eyes often come out with particular distinctness due to mechanical registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument choice: stereoscope limitations and double-image prism preference
rubrics_metrics.description: The stereoscope affords a very easy method of optically superimposing two portraits, but it is a makeshift and imperfect way; the best instrument used is a 'double-image prism' of Iceland spar which creates true optical combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereoscope places two images for the brain to combine and may produce variable vividness between eyes. Double-image prisms, glass/mirror arrangements, divided lenses, or multiple prisms produce true optical superimposition and allow more precise adjustment of divergence, achromaticity, and overlap. Choose instrument according to number of images and desired optical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining differing sizes, foreshortening and focus tolerances
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraits of somewhat different sizes may be combined by placing the larger one farther from the eye, and a long face may be fitted to a short one by inclining and foreshortening the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight faults of focus from adjusting distance/foreshortening produce little or no sensible ill-effect on appearance of the composite. Use adjustable frames, lenses of different powers, mirrors for reflection, or move portraits nearer/farther as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended attitudes and sizing for family composites
rubrics_metrics.description: For family composites the size suggested is that which gives one-half of an inch interval between the pupil of the eye and the line that separates the two lips. The attitudes recommended: full face, an exact profile (always showing the right side), and an exact three-quarters (always showing the left) with the outer edge of the right eyelid only just in sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect sets of family photographs all nearly the same size and taken in the same attitudes (full face, exact profile right, exact three-quarters left) to facilitate accurate composites. These positions are well suited to cartes-de-visite format and to consistent registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genealogical weighting scheme for parental/kin composites
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested weights: weight each parent as 4; each grandparent and each uncle and aunt as 1; weight each brother and sister as 4; weight those cousins who inherited any part of the family likeness as 1; disregard other cousins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply weights by giving proportionate exposure times. The scheme is proposed as an initial convention for pedigree composites; it can be adjusted as better statistical data become available. The author suggests equal weighting of male and female sides for early trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of components and repeatability (robustness to component order)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several components are combined the composite is substantially the average; trials with three portraits in all six possible orders showed four of the six composites closely alike. The composite of many components represents no man in particular but portrays an imaginary figure possessing the average features of any given group of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of photographing components should not materially affect result if equal exposures are used. Repeat trials with different batches/batches orders to test the stability and truth of pictorial deductions; substantial agreement across batches is a test of statistical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses and limitations of composites (typology, likeness, heredity, historical reconstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses: to give typical pictures of different races, to select prevalent/strongly-marked types (e.g., criminal types), to obtain a really good likeness of a living person by combining many photographs taken at different times, to produce the most probable likeness of a historical personage from statues/medals/photographs, and to investigate hereditary transmission by comparing averages of product and parentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in interpretation: composites represent an average or 'type', not an individual. For heredity work include appropriate relatives (parents, grandparents, uncles/aunts, siblings, relevant cousins) and apply weights; compare composites of products and parental sets to investigate hereditary resemblance. Use multiple independent batches to corroborate pictorial deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical superimposition variants and exhibition methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Many methods: double-image prisms (one behind another for multiple images), glass inclined with a mirror producing two rays, additional pieces of glass at varying inclinations for more portraits, divided lenses, sextants with telescope, strips of mirrors, multiple magic-lanterns converging on same screen, dioramic apparatus, or a camera with many slightly-divergent object-glasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select method according to number of images, need for exhibition, and available illumination (electric light + screen may allow immediate photographic capture). Multiple prisms may produce 4 images (useful) but more (e.g., 8) may reduce distinctness; balance number of components with optical clarity.
